instructions: Pat the salmon dry and cut it into 4 equal fillets if it isn't already. In a small bowl, stir the Dijon mustard, 1/2 tsp of the salt and the pepper with the olive oil into a loose paste. Spread it over the top of each fillet.
Finely dice the shallots. Pull the thick stems off the sorrel and slice the leaves into ribbons about 1/2 inch wide.
Melt the butter in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Add the shallots and cook for 3 minutes, until they're soft and not browned.
Add the sorrel a big handful at a time, stirring until each handful wilts. In 2 to 3 minutes it will turn an olive green and fall apart into a soft purée. That color is normal.
Turn the heat to low and stir in the creme fraiche, 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1/2 tsp of the salt. Warm it for 2 minutes, stirring, and don't let it boil. Take it off the heat and cover it.
Heat a large nonstick skillet over medium-high. Add the salmon paste side down. Cook for 3 minutes, until the paste side is golden.
Flip the fillets, turn the heat down to medium-low, cover the pan and cook for 5 to 6 minutes. The salmon is done when it flakes easily at the thickest part.
Warm the sauce over low heat for 1 minute if it has cooled. Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt or a little more lemon juice.
Spoon the sauce onto the plates and set the salmon on top.
method_notes: Perfectly Provence's Saumon a la Creme d'Oseille is the lead: shallots softened in butter, sorrel and creme fraiche with lemon, and salmon seared with a Dijon paste. Its page shows no rating, so this is a fallback lead. Pierre Franey's version thickens the sauce with egg yolks and dredges the salmon in flour, so it was not followed (flour would also break gluten-free). The lead blanches the sorrel and blends the sauce; here the sorrel is wilted straight in the butter and stirred smooth, which saves a pot and an ice bath. The braised radishes in the lead are left out. Sorrel can be hard to find, so check for it at a farmers market or a well-stocked grocery.
